quiz.q: Why is `Instant` preferred over `SystemTime` for measuring elapsed time?
options: Instant is monotonic and immune to system clock changes; SystemTime can jump
Instant returns a Result while SystemTime doesn't
quiz.explain: Instant only ever moves forward and ignores clock adjustments, making it the right tool for timing code.
elapsed() gives you a Duration — how much time has passed since the Instant was captured.

quiz.q: Why does `SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH)` return a `Result` instead of a bare `Duration`?
options: Because UNIX_EPOCH might not exist on some platforms
Because a Duration can never be negative, but the wall clock could theoretically be set before the reference time
Because duration_since always panics if called twice
Because Result is required for any function used in main
quiz.explain: Duration can't represent negative time, and a real wall clock can go backward relative to a reference point — so the API returns Err instead of pretending.

quiz.q: Which crate provides real calendar dates, timezones, and formatting in Rust?
quiz.explain: std has no calendar type at all — chrono is the ecosystem standard for actual dates, timezones, and formatting/parsing.

quiz.q: What's wrong with calling `.format("%Y-%m-%d")` on an `Instant`?
options: Instant has no .format method — it's an opaque stopwatch reading with no calendar meaning
It only works on chrono::Local values
quiz.explain: Instant isn't tied to any calendar date at all, so it has no .format method. Formatting is a chrono DateTime operation.

quiz.q: What's the difference between `%m` and `%M` in a chrono format string?
quiz.explain: One letter's case flips the whole field — %m is the month, %M is minutes. Worth double-checking against real output.

quiz.q: Why be careful comparing `DateTime<Utc>` and `DateTime<Local>` directly?
options: They can never be compared — it's a compile error
They represent the same instant differently depending on machine timezone, causing off-by-hours bugs if not converted first
Local time is always computed faster
chrono has deprecated the Local type
quiz.explain: Comparing across timezones without normalizing to the same one first is a classic source of subtle bugs.

quiz.q: Which type would you reach for to time how long a function call takes?
quiz.explain: Instant + .elapsed() is built specifically for measuring durations, immune to wall-clock adjustments.

flashcards.back: A monotonic measurement of elapsed time, immune to system clock changes — use it for timing code.
Real wall-clock time, which can jump if the system clock is adjusted — use it for timestamps, not measuring durations.

flashcards.front: Why does duration_since return a Result?
flashcards.back: Because a Duration can never be negative, and a wall clock can genuinely go backward relative to a reference point.

flashcards.front: What calendar features does std::time provide?
flashcards.back: None — no year, month, day, or timezone. For real calendar dates, use the chrono crate.
A DateTime<Utc> — a real calendar timestamp that knows its own timezone.

flashcards.front: How do you format a chrono DateTime as text?
flashcards.back: Call .format("%Y-%m-%d") (or any strftime-style pattern) on it.

flashcards.front: What's a classic timezone bug to watch for?
flashcards.back: Comparing a Utc time to a Local time directly without converting one to match the other first.
